details.description of steps: Planned a torch DataLoader wrapper around the HF dataset (map-style + optional streaming, num_workers, pin_memory, prefetch_factor, persistent_workers, convert('RGB') transform, optional CUDA prefetcher).
details.prompt:
In my last exercise I loaded a dataset completly in memory:

df = load_dataset(HG_DATASET).shuffle(seed=SEED)
train_data = df["train"]

As this might not scale well for bigger tasks and the fact that there is no preproc done. Can you write me a torch data loader class that does prefetching , pins memeory etc. As preproc apply

.convert("RGB")
details.location_of_edit: Planned and proposed code for HFImageDataset.
details.knowledge_extracted: Planned design: torch Dataset wrapping HF dataset with on-the-fly convert('RGB'); DataLoader(num_workers>0, pin_memory=True, prefetch_factor, persistent_workers=True); streaming=True avoids downloading the whole dataset (HF IterableDataset splits shards across workers); PIL images of different sizes need a resize/transform or a list-collate before batching; non_blocking .to(device) benefits from pinned memory. Note: non-streaming load_dataset memory-maps Arrow files from disk rather than holding everything in RAM.

details.description of steps: Reviewed the user's HFImageDataset + DataLoader code from knowledge of PyTorch multiprocessing (no error message given); identified the likely Windows-specific cause and other issues, gave a fixed version.
details.prompt: class HFImageDataset(Dataset): ... (HF dataset wrapper with convert('RGB'), custom_collate_fn returning the list, DataLoader with num_workers/pin_memory/prefetch_factor in an if/else) Is this a windows specific problem? Something with multiworker?
details.location_of_edit: HFImageDataset class, custom_collate_fn and the DataLoader construction (if NUM_WORKER > 0 / else block).
details.knowledge_extracted: Yes, very likely Windows: DataLoader workers use 'spawn' there (not fork), so each worker re-imports __main__ and must unpickle the Dataset, collate_fn and transform. Classes/functions defined in a Jupyter notebook cannot be found by the worker (AttributeError: Can't get attribute 'HFImageDataset' on <module '__main__'> or hanging) -> move them into a .py module and import them; in scripts guard with if __name__ == '__main__'; no lambdas as transform. persistent_workers=True avoids slow re-spawning every epoch. Other notes: pin_memory has no effect on lists of PIL images (only tensors) -> pin after converting to tensors; shuffle=False loses the earlier shuffling; the if/else can be collapsed by only adding prefetch_factor/persistent_workers when num_workers > 0.

details.description of steps: Answered from knowledge of the transformers / open_clip / openai-clip APIs: how to read the tokenizer vocabulary and the token embedding matrix, plus how to turn vocabulary tokens into joint-space embeddings.
details.prompt: How do I get access to the vocabulary of a trained CLIP model?
details.location_of_edit: No file edited; snippets in chat.
details.knowledge_extracted: CLIP uses a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 49,408 tokens (incl. <|startoftext|>=49406, <|endoftext|>=49407); '</w>' marks word-final tokens. HF: CLIPTokenizer.from_pretrained(name).get_vocab() -> {token: id}; input token embeddings: model.text_model.embeddings.token_embedding.weight (49408 x text width, 512 for B/32 & B/16, 768 for L/14). open_clip: open_clip.get_tokenizer(name).encoder / model.token_embedding.weight. Vocabulary = subword pieces, not words; token embeddings are NOT in the joint image-text space -> to compare with images run tokens (e.g. whole-word tokens ending in '</w>', ~30k) through the text encoder via model.get_text_features in batches. SigLIP uses a different (SentencePiece) tokenizer.

details.description of steps: Analyzed the user's PEZ (hard-prompt optimization) draft: all runs (classes x variants x seeds) were optimized sequentially with batch size 1 through the CLIP text encoder, plus an extra forward pass at every eval. Rewrote it so that all runs are optimized in parallel as one batch (P: (R, M, d_tok)), with a vectorized loss and per-run best-prompt tracking. Not executed (no torch available in the sandbox; the user stopped the install earlier).
details.prompt: I think I have a working solution. But it is extreeeemly slow. I waited over a hour for the optimization to finsih. Can you rewrite my draft so that it uses batch mode? (code: _inject_hook forward hook on token_emb, dummy_ids, encode_prompt_embeds, encode_text, targets/centroids/surr_dir per class, VARIANTS + prompt_loss (attraction, CE vs sibling centroid, surrogate direction), pez() optimization loop, evaluate() + loop over CLASSES x VARIANTS x seeds)
details.location_of_edit: _inject_hook (now supports per-row P of shape (R, M, d)), dummy_ids (batch dim R), encode_prompt_embeds -> encode_prompt_embeds_batch, new stacked class tensors (TGT, CEN, SIB, SUR), prompt_loss -> prompt_loss_batch (returns per-run loss), pez -> pez_batch(runs), evaluation loop (one call for all runs + batched encode_text).
details.knowledge_extracted: Main cause of slowness: R = |CLASSES|*3*3 independent runs x 3000 steps, each a batch-1 forward+backward through the text encoder plus a redundant re-encode at every eval. Since runs don't interact, they can be stacked: summing per-run losses gives each P_r exactly its own gradient, and AdamW works elementwise, so it is equivalent to separate runs (except different random batch sampling). Further speedups: clip_backbone.eval().requires_grad_(False) (no gradients for CLIP weights), build dummy ids once, reuse t from the forward pass for eval, fewer .item() syncs; optional bf16 autocast. The forward hook must be removed and registered again after redefining _inject_hook. Requires that all classes have the same TOP_K targets (for torch.stack) and that project() works on (N, d).

details.description of steps: Loaded the dataviz skill, validated a 3-color categorical palette with its validator (pass; contrast warning -> direct labels + table view), wrote plot_loss.py with matplotlib small multiples, tested it on synthetic histories, inspected the rendered PNG and fixed overlapping end labels.
details.prompt: Can you code me a visulaization that displays th eloss curves, we have tracked?
details.location_of_edit: New file plot_loss.py: histories_to_df (histories dict -> long DataFrame), plot_loss_curves (rows = classes, columns = metrics, mean over seeds + min-max band, colored + line-styled per variant, collision-aware direct labels, optional noisy batch_loss), final_summary (table of final/best loss & attraction per class x variant).
details.knowledge_extracted: The 'loss' values are not comparable across variants (different loss weights A1/A2/A3 add terms), so compare variants on the 'attract' metric (shared L1 term) and use 'loss' only for convergence within a variant. Mean over seeds + min-max band shows seed variance without spaghetti lines. Color + line style per variant makes it readable without color; direct labels only when they don't overlap.

Notebook cell: load StableDiffusionPipeline, select A3 prompts from df_res.
details.knowledge_extracted: Verification loop: optimized hard prompt -> text-to-image -> closed-box API checks whether the prompt really encodes the class concept. SD 2.1 uses an OpenCLIP ViT-H text encoder, i.e. a different text encoder than the local CLIP used for PEZ, so this also tests whether the prompts transfer across models (gibberish tokens often don't). Fixed per-image generator seeds make results reproducible; saving PNGs avoids regenerating. Response format of the API is unknown -> parse_scores handles dict {class: score}, {'scores'|'probabilities'|...: ...} or a list aligned with CLASSES.

details.description of steps: Extended the user's batched PEZ loss with a fourth term (multi-class contrastive loss against all class centroids), using the 4th weight of VARIANTS; ran the palette validator for a 4th plot color (A4) for plot_loss.py.
details.prompt: VARIANTS = {A1..A4 with 4 weights}, TAU = 0.05, RUNS/TGT/COWN/CSIB/SDIR/W stacked per run, batched_loss(t, tgt) with att + con (own vs sibling CE) + sur. I began to add a forth loss. This time I also want to penalize closeness to any other class. So that e.g. class 1 should be maximized, while any other class should be minimized
details.location_of_edit: Setup cell after RUNS/TGT/... (new tensors CALL (all class centroids) and OWN_IDX per run), batched_loss (new term L4 = CE over all centroids, weighted by W[:, 3]); plot_loss.py VARIANT_STYLE (A4 entry).
details.knowledge_extracted: L4 = multi-class InfoNCE/softmax CE: logits = t·c_j / TAU for all class centroids j, target = own class -> pulls t to its own centroid and pushes it from all others; with small TAU the softmax concentrates on the closest (hardest) negatives. L2 is the 2-class special case (own vs sibling), so A4 weights the sibling twice (intended or set w_con=0 to isolate L4). Alternative: use the surrogate head directions of the other classes as negatives (closer to what the closed box decides). Add A4 to the plot styles (4th validated color #eda100, dotted).

details.description of steps: Rewrote the L4 term to use the surrogate head directions of all classes as the softmax logits instead of the image centroids; added an optional modality-gap correction because L4 compares scores across classes.
details.prompt: That is a great catch! Use the surrogate head direction
details.location_of_edit: Setup cell (SALL = stacked surr_dir of all classes, OWN_IDX, TAU_SUR, optional MU_IMG/MU_TXT gap vectors) and batched_loss (L4 = CE over t_img @ SALL.T / TAU_SUR).
details.knowledge_extracted: L4 with surrogate directions: logits_j = t·s_j / TAU_SUR, target = own class -> maximizes the own decision direction relative to all others (closer to what the closed box decides than centroids). surr_dir only exists for CLASSES, so only those are negatives. Modality gap matters here: the head directions were fit on image embeddings, a text embedding has a gap offset Δ that adds a class-dependent constant s_j·Δ to each logit -> biases the softmax across classes (unlike L3, where it is a per-class constant). Fix: score t_img = normalize(t − μ_txt + μ_img). Cosines between text features and head directions are often small, so TAU_SUR may need separate tuning. If two classes share a head with opposite sign, s_other = −s_own, so the CE term is consistent with L3.

details.description of steps: Answered from knowledge of PyTorch CUDA memory management.
details.prompt: How do I clear my gpu memory after image generation again?
details.location_of_edit: No file edited; cell after generate_and_query / the Stable Diffusion step.
details.knowledge_extracted: Delete all references to the pipeline (del pipe, plus any other variable holding it or its outputs/tensors), run gc.collect() so Python frees the objects, then torch.cuda.empty_cache() to return cached blocks to the driver; check with torch.cuda.memory_allocated()/memory_reserved(). In Jupyter, hidden references (Out[], _, exception tracebacks) can keep objects alive. Alternative: pipe.to('cpu') or enable_model_cpu_offload(). Restarting the kernel is the only guaranteed full reset.
